subtype: Approach: ignore the notice as spam [Pitfall]
passage:
To: Jaya, Customer Support
Subject: Help after data leak

Dear Jaya,

I'm writing because I did the wrong thing. On 4 February your company sent an email saying some customer details had leaked. It looked like junk, so I deleted it without reading past the first line.

Six weeks later I began getting calls from people who knew my name and the address I gave you, saying they were from my delivery service. I lost a whole afternoon and gave one of them a code before I realised something was off.

Could you tell me what exactly was in the leak, and whether anything can still be done? I know I waited too long.

Mohit

Reply: "We're sorry. We will help, though the delay does make tracing harder."

qa.q: On what date did the company send the notice?
What was Mohit feeling when writing that the wrong thing was done?
qa.a: Mohit felt regret and worry, blaming the delay in reading the notice and realising too late that the calls were a trick.

qa.q: What could Mohit do now besides asking the company, and why?
qa.a: Mohit could tell the bank and keep a record of the calls, because reporting quickly and keeping details helps others trace what happened.

qa.q: How might Jaya see Mohit's email?
qa.a: Jaya may see a customer who is embarrassed but honest, and would want to help while knowing the six-week gap limits what can be traced.

grounding: The user assumes the breach email is junk and deletes it, then weeks later phishing calls use the leaked details, and the delay makes tracing harder.
